texts.intro: You will hear a father talking to his children about the plans for a birthday celebration.
lines: Meena, Sanjay, your mom's birthday is coming soon. Shall we celebrate it at her favourite restaurant?
Well, we went there recently. How about a surprise celebration at home?
Or, why not try an outdoor celebration at the beach?
That sounds fun but the weather can be unpredictable at this time of the year. I prefer Meena's idea. What presents are you giving her?
I'm getting a purse for her!
She likes the one she's using now. What about a bottle of perfume instead?
I had considered that but the purse she's using now looks old.
Perfume is pricey. So, I'll get her a pair of sunglasses. What about you, Dad?
Erm, I was deciding between a cookbook and a watch.
That's easy! Mom already has a few watches. Besides, we can eat what she cooks!
You're right! I'll get the birthday cake too!

texts.intro: You will hear two friends talking about the Co-curricular Activities Open House at the entrance to the school hall.
lines: Hi, Jenny! I'm excited to choose my co-curricular activity today! I'll visit the Boy Scouts booth first because I'm keen to join a uniformed group. Then, I'll visit the Science Club because it deals with my favourite subject. I'll decide after that and indicate my choices on the option form.
I'm excited too, Yazid! I'm considering the Drama Club but my parents suggested the Girl Guides.
Shall we check out the uniformed groups together? From there, we'll go to the next booth that interests us. I heard we can collect nice bookmarks at each booth.
Ok, but I want to use the coupon in the welcome pack to collect the refreshment first.
Oh, I haven't collected my welcome pack yet. I was going to look for our Form Teacher to get the option form.
Let me help you collect the welcome pack. I'll see you at the booths for uniformed groups after I've exchanged our coupons for refreshment.
Thanks, Jenny. By the way, do you have a pen to fill in the option form? I forgot to bring mine.
There's one in the welcome pack. It also provides a brochure that gives information about the co-curricular activities.

texts.intro: You will hear an extract from a radio programme.
lines: In today's segment of Encounter with Animals, a listener, Jane, called our radio station to share her encounter with a monkey. Let's hear her story.

Yesterday, I noticed rubbish around the bin outside my house. I wasn't alarmed as it's common for monkeys from the nearby forest to ransack the bins. When I went to the kitchen, I discovered my cake missing. I thought I'd placed it elsewhere, that is until I spotted tiny paw prints. Before I could react, a monkey suddenly leapt out and scared the daylights out of me! I screamed as it ran around the kitchen! I panicked and grabbed a broom. I hit the floor with it, hoping to scare the monkey. Perhaps, threatened by the noise, the monkey scratched my hand before scuttling away through the open window. On hindsight, it would've been better if I'd run out of the kitchen.

My neighbour said that having a dog has helped to keep monkeys away from her house. My family isn't keen, although I like that idea. I asked a National Parks spokesperson about how to handle such a situation. He advised me to close all windows when no one's home or to install window grilles. Sigh, since I can be absent-minded at times, I know what I should do now...

texts.intro: You will hear an extract from a news report.
lines: This year's recipient of the Exemplary Educator Award is Mrs Tania Lee. She is one of the few who received many nominations. Mrs Lee, who is coincidentally receiving the Long Service Award for twenty years of service in education, stands out with her readiness to go the extra mile for her students.
This is what one of her students, John, said,

I used to think I was hopeless in Maths and found it hard to follow the lessons. But Mrs Lee taught me not to give up easily. She used lots of real-life examples to help us understand Maths. She gave some of us extra coaching. With more practice, I started to improve. Now, I can even coach others who are weak in Maths!

I know John has the potential to perform better. Many teachers told me they enjoyed teaching him because he's hardworking. I'm proud of his progress and have entrusted him with the responsibility to help the weaker ones. Some people have asked me how to be a good teacher. I tell them it's not easy to be one. But what keeps me going is my love for teaching. If we enjoy what we do, work will not become a chore. Naturally, I'm glad when my students tell me I've inspired them to chase their dreams.

texts.intro: You will hear a TV host interviewing a young hawker.
lines: Let's welcome Billy Wong, a 28-year-old hawker. Billy, tell us why you've become a hawker.

I love eating at hawker centres! It's a special place where I bond with family and friends over delicious and affordable food. Unfortunately, many young people nowadays think otherwise. I wish to play a part in helping them appreciate the hawker food culture. It wasn't until my grandma gave me her secret recipe for chicken rice that I decided to become a hawker so that I can fulfill that wish.
What is it like being a hawker?

Oh, standing in front of the hot stove is uncomfortable but I'm used to it by now. Imagine working 12 hours daily! Do you know that a day as a hawker is similar to an intense workout at the gym? I wonder how I'll sustain this hectic work as I age. We also can't please everyone who tastes our food. While complaints discourage me, compliments make my day.
Do you have any advice for aspiring hawkers?

Firstly, if you're inexperienced, start small so that you don't need to invest too much money. When I first started, I struggled to make enough to cover expenses. My business improved later on and I'm earning much more now than from my previous job. So don't give up. Your efforts will be rewarded if you improve your recipe by listening to what people say about your food. Give it a try! No pain, no gain. You may even become a famous hawker one day!

texts.intro: You will hear a story about how a girl saved her brother.
lines: Eric's father helped a rich man to look after his goats.

One day, Eric's father fell ill. Eric had to cancel his fishing trip with his friends to take the goats to graze on the mountain. He had never done it before. Nevertheless, he put on a brave front so that his family would not worry about him. His sister, Dina, assured him by saying,
You can do it! I'll join you on the mountain at lunchtime and get you some food to eat.

When lunch was ready, Dina went up the mountain to look for Eric. However, she was surprised the goats were left unattended. She knew Eric was not the sort to run off to play, though he might have gone to look for her when he became hungry. Thinking that he might be wandering around, she searched for him. She ended up at the cave where a monster lived. When she saw her brother's hat at the cave entrance, she feared the worst. Unsure if he had been captured by the monster, she decided to search the cave.

When Dina did not see Eric in the cave, she felt relieved. She was about to leave when she heard Eric's muffled moaning. Her blood grew cold. Dina was determined to save him even if it meant risking her own life. As an idea had come to her, she reached for the basket of food.
A moment later, Dina found the monster and said,
Oh mighty master, your humble servant has brought delicious food for you. Please accept my offering.
The monster swallowed the food greedily and collapsed in a heap, not knowing that poisonous mushrooms had been added to the food. Seizing the chance, the siblings escaped from the monster.

texts.intro: You will hear an extract from a talk.
lines: If you're at the Pinnacle Park on a Monday morning, you'll be greeted by an unusual sight of some adults pretending to brush their teeth, wash their faces and comb their hair, while laughing heartily. They seem to be rehearsing for a play but they're actually having their laughter session. Led by Mr Mohan, a certified trainer, they're practising different types of laughter, together with some stretching and breathing techniques. Believing that laughter is the best medicine, Mr Mohan formed this Laughter Club.

He took some time to persuade people to buy into the idea. Most participants found it strange to laugh without reason. Although some of them tried to cover their mouths while laughing, they're still self-conscious when practising it outdoors. Laughing in a group helps as they can tease one another to lighten the atmosphere.

Participants feel more refreshed and energetic after each session. Indeed, laughter strengthens our immunity as well as enhances our emotional and mental health. These positive effects have helped the club grow in number. Sharing a good laugh with friends also improves relationships. Best of all, laughter is fun and free!

I prefer Meena's idea.
qs.why: Both the restaurant and the beach are rejected: they went to the restaurant recently (Meena), and the weather at the beach is unpredictable (Father). Father says 'I prefer Meena's idea', which is a surprise celebration at home.
qs.stem: Where will the family celebrate Mother's birthday?
qs.key: How about a surprise celebration at home?

keys: I'm getting a purse for her!
So, I'll get her a pair of sunglasses.
Mom already has a few watches.
qs.why: Everyone's first idea gets changed: perfume is pricey and Mom already has a few watches. The gifts are Meena's purse, Sanjay's sunglasses, and Dad's cookbook (he chose between a cookbook and a watch). The cake is not in the pictures.
qs.stem: What will Mother receive for her birthday?
qs.key: I'm getting a purse for her!

keys: Then, I'll visit the Science Club because it deals with my favourite subject.
Shall we check out the uniformed groups together?
I want to use the coupon in the welcome pack to collect the refreshment first.
Let me help you collect the welcome pack.
qs.why: Jenny's order: entrance → collection point to help Yazid get his welcome pack → refreshment booth to exchange coupons → the uniformed groups (Boy Scouts, Girl Guides) → the next booth they like (Science Club). The dashed line is the only one that goes through all of these. The dotted line skips the uniformed groups, and the solid line skips the refreshment booth.
qs.stem: Which of the three lines shows the route that Jenny will take?
qs.key: Then, I'll visit the Science Club because it deals with my favourite subject.

keys: I heard we can collect nice bookmarks at each booth.
I want to use the coupon in the welcome pack to collect the refreshment first.
I was going to look for our Form Teacher to get the option form.

qs.key: I heard we can collect nice bookmarks at each booth.

keys: I wasn't alarmed as it's common for monkeys from the nearby forest to ransack the bins.
When I went to the kitchen, I discovered my cake missing.
qs.why: The question asks when Jane FIRST sensed something was wrong. She was not alarmed by the rubbish outside. She began to feel something was off when she found her cake missing, so the answer is the empty cake box. The paw prints came after that.
qs.stem: Which picture shows the time when Jane first sensed something was amiss?
qs.key: I wasn't alarmed as it's common for monkeys from the nearby forest to ransack the bins.

keys: On hindsight, it would've been better if I'd run out of the kitchen.
qs.why: The question asks what she SHOULD have done, not what she did. She hit the floor with a broom and was scratched. 'On hindsight' tells you the better choice: run out of the kitchen.
qs.stem: What should Jane have done when she encountered the monkey?
qs.key: On hindsight, it would've been better if I'd run out of the kitchen.

qs.key: But what keeps me going is my love for teaching.

qs.key: Oh, standing in front of the hot stove is uncomfortable but I'm used to it by now.

qs.key: Firstly, if you're inexperienced, start small so that you don't need to invest too much money.

opts: He was unsure as he was inexperienced.
He was unwilling to go to the mountain alone.
He was upset as he could not go fishing with friends.

qs.stem: What was Dina's first thought when she found Eric missing?
qs.key: She knew Eric was not the sort to run off to play, though he might have gone to look for her when he became hungry.

qs.why: When she saw his hat she only feared the worst and was still unsure. She searched the cave and saw nothing. Only when she heard his muffled moaning was she certain he was in the cave.
qs.stem: Dina became certain of where Eric was when she ______.
qs.key: When she saw her brother's hat at the cave entrance, she feared the worst. Unsure if he had been captured by the monster, she decided to search the cave.

qs.why: The question asks which quality HELPED her save Eric. It was her idea (pretending to be a servant and adding poisonous mushrooms to the food) that saved him, so the answer is cleverness. Selflessness is her attitude, but it is not what rescued him.
qs.stem: Which quality helped Dina to save Eric?
qs.key: Dina was determined to save him even if it meant risking her own life.

have their laughing session indoors

texts.intro: You will hear Lisa and her father talking about what to buy.
lines: Dad, what are we having for dinner tonight?
Let's see what we have in the fridge. Oh dear! We only have some eggs. I think I'll need to make a trip to the supermarket to get some fresh vegetables.
I saw that the carton of milk was almost empty when I had some for breakfast this morning. Maybe we could get some milk as well?
All right! And I'll get my favourite brand of ice cream since it's just at the next section. We have strawberries in the fridge to go with it.
Could I get a ride from you, Dad? I need to pass these books to Jenny. Do you think we could stop by her place after going to the supermarket?
Let's do that before we get the groceries, so we don't keep her waiting.
Oh yes, remind me to pick up the special cat food for Jingle after we are done at the supermarket. The pet shop called to say the cat food has arrived. That would be our last stop.
All right, Dad! I'm sure we'll be home before the ice cream melts!

texts.intro: You will hear two children discussing where to go for lunch.
lines: Wei Kang had just moved into a new neighbourhood. His helpful neighbour, Priya, offered to show him around. Their first stop was the community club as Wei Kang was eager to find out if they conducted taekwondo classes. After finding out more about the various programmes available there, the children felt hungry and decided to grab a bite.
"Priya, where is a good place to have lunch?" asked Wei Kang.

"Well, there is a food centre nearby. There's also a café not too far away. But I was thinking that we could grab a bite after I show you where the swimming complex is. I hear they conduct water-safety classes there," Priya pointed out.

"If we were to have lunch at the food centre, we need to turn right at the swimming complex and we'll come to an overhead bridge. After crossing it, we would be able to see the food centre. But if we want to go to the café, we need to turn left at the swimming complex," Priya explained.
"Shall we eat at the food centre?" Wei Kang asked.
"That's fine with me. I think there is another route we can take which is shorter. We can cut across the playground at Block 24 to reach there faster," said Priya.
After some discussion, the children decided against taking that route as Wei Kang wanted to see more of the neighbourhood.
"By the way, there's a taekwondo class later. I'd like to check it out. Can we come back here at 4 p.m.?" Wei Kang asked just as they were about to leave the community club.
"Sure!" Priya said. "We can visit the café another time then."

texts.intro: You will hear an account of Mr Ong participating in a health screening session.
lines: One afternoon, Mr Ong headed for the nearby community club where there was free health screening for senior citizens. When he entered the hall of the community club, he saw that it was divided into several stations. At each station was a Health Officer who took care of specific tasks, such as measuring blood pressure or testing eyesight.
Mr Ong walked to the registration counter which was nearest the entrance. There, a Health Officer took down his personal particulars.
Mr Ong then went to the first health screening station where another Health Officer checked his eyesight.
"Will my height and weight be measured too?" asked Mr Ong. "Oh yes! Right after this station. Following that, you'll have your blood pressure taken at the last station," the Health Officer explained.

After completing the health screening, Mr Ong was guided to an area nearest the exit for a talk on growing old healthily. After the talk, Mr Ong resolved to quit smoking, resume exercising and avoid heavy meals.

texts.intro: You will hear Sarah giving a presentation to her class.
lines: Good morning, everyone! For Show-and-Tell today, I've brought along two postcards on the Jody River. I started collecting old postcards when my grandfather first gave me one dating back to the 1920s.

Let's look at the first postcard. It shows a scene of the Jody River. Can you see these boats along the river? We don't see them anymore. What we have now are river taxis which tourists can board for a short ride along the Jody River, and during the cruise, they can admire the National Theatre and the newly constructed Arts Centre. Long ago, boats were used to transport goods such as rice, which would then be unloaded into warehouses along the river like you see here. These warehouses of long ago have all been converted into shops, restaurants and banks.

All right, let's look at the second postcard. It shows the Clarkson Building along the Jody River. It was built in the 1920s and used to be a school, but now it's been converted into a hotel which is popular with tourists.
I've come to the end of my presentation. I hope you like it. Thank you.

texts.intro: This is an extract of a documentary on fire ants.
lines: Are you able to carry a load that is ten times your weight? Fire ants can do so! They are incredibly strong and have amazing teamwork. By working together, they can very quickly bring down an insect many times their size. Fire ants are also well-organised. During a flood, entire fire ant colonies can clump together and float until they find a new home. Fire ants have a keen sense of touch. The slightest disturbance to their nest will cause them to release chemical signals to warn one another so they can put up a defence within seconds.

Fire ants attack by injecting a poisonous sting which causes a burning sensation, a painful reminder of how fire ants got their name. These fiery stings have made the insect widely feared. However, fire ants are more annoying than dangerous as people generally recover from these stings. The damage fire ants cause to homes and electrical equipment is much more serious. Yet, totally eradicating these insects is impossible.

texts.intro: You will hear a story about a soldier and an old woman.
lines: There once lived a kind-hearted queen who freely gave out rice to the poor villagers in her land. Every week, her soldiers would deliver the sacks of rice to the needy and each soldier would give a report to the queen when they returned. In this way, the queen knew if they had carried out her orders faithfully.

When the queen grew old, she asked her son, Prince Lawrence, to continue her work. Unlike the queen, Prince Lawrence was lazy and impatient. He did away with listening to the soldiers' weekly reports. "Such a waste of my precious time!" he moaned.

One of the soldiers, Jasper, was very happy with this change. "I can now take some of the rice for myself without having to account for it," Jasper thought. "I will only take a little once in a while and keep it for myself." At first, that was what Jasper did. However, stealing the rice soon became a habit he could not stop. Jasper even sold the rice at a high price to the needy.
"Why are you fattening yourself at our expense? The rice is supposed to be free!" a small, old woman confronted Jasper when he came by to sell the rice he had stolen.
"Goodness! You do have a loud voice for one so tiny!" Jasper ridiculed the old woman and waved her away.
Months later, a famine struck the land and food became scarce. Many went hungry, including Jasper.

One day, when Jasper was scavenging for food, someone tapped him on his shoulder. He spun around to see an old woman offering him a small bag of rice. It was the same old woman whom Jasper had met before. In a quivering voice, Jasper asked, "Why are you giving me food when I denied you of it in the past?"
The old woman replied, "The Queen freely gave us food over the years. How could I not freely share it with you now?"

texts.intro: You will hear an extract from a radio programme.
lines: Do you know that the benefits of being grateful are supported by scientific evidence? In today's programme, I'm going to share with you some of these studies which show that being grateful has its advantages.

Some researchers found that being grateful can help us to be happier. How is this so? Well, when you are grateful, you are less likely to feel jealous or angry, and as a result, you would feel happier. Some studies also show that people who have a grateful attitude recover more quickly from difficulties and suffering.

So then, how can we learn to be grateful? To illustrate, let me share with you a story about Ronnie. Every night, Ronnie would reflect on his day and ask himself what he was grateful for. For each thing or person he was grateful for, he would put a coin into a little box. When it became full, Ronnie would empty the coins and donate them to charity.
Well, I hope my little story will encourage you to learn how to be a grateful person. Bye-bye!

That would be our last stop.

qs.key: Let's do that before we get the groceries, so we don't keep her waiting.

qs.key: But I was thinking that we could grab a bite after I show you where the swimming complex is.

qs.why: The first station checks eyesight. The second station (right after it) measures height and weight, and the last station takes blood pressure. The second picture shows someone standing on the weighing scale.
qs.stem: Which picture shows what happened at the second health screening station?
qs.key: Mr Ong then went to the first health screening station where another Health Officer checked his eyesight.

keys: Mr Ong walked to the registration counter which was nearest the entrance.
Following that, you'll have your blood pressure taken at the last station
After completing the health screening, Mr Ong was guided to an area nearest the exit for a talk on growing old healthily.
qs.why: Near the entrance is the registration counter, and near the exit is the area for the talk. Neither is for blood pressure. Blood pressure is taken at the last of the three stations.
qs.stem: Where should Mr Ong go to check his blood pressure?
qs.key: Mr Ong walked to the registration counter which was nearest the entrance.

keys: After the talk, Mr Ong resolved to quit smoking, resume exercising and avoid heavy meals.
qs.why: All three are mentioned, so listen for the verbs. Quit smoking and avoid heavy meals are about NOT doing something. Only 'resume exercising' is something he starts doing again, so the answer is exercise.
qs.stem: What did Mr Ong decide to start doing again after attending the talk?
qs.key: After the talk, Mr Ong resolved to quit smoking, resume exercising and avoid heavy meals.

opts: sightseeing
carrying goods
ferrying people
keys: Long ago, boats were used to transport goods such as rice, which would then be unloaded into warehouses along the river like you see here.
qs.why: In the past the boats were used to transport goods such as rice. The river taxis today are the ones that take tourists sightseeing.
qs.stem: What were the boats used for in the past?
qs.key: Long ago, boats were used to transport goods such as rice, which would then be unloaded into warehouses along the river like you see here.

opts: residential purposes
educational purposes
commercial purposes
keys: These warehouses of long ago have all been converted into shops, restaurants and banks.
qs.why: The warehouses have been converted into shops, restaurants and banks, which are commercial uses. The educational use belongs to the Clarkson Building, which used to be a school and is now a hotel.
qs.stem: The warehouses are now used for ______.
qs.key: These warehouses of long ago have all been converted into shops, restaurants and banks.

opts: her interest in collecting postcards on the Jody River
tourist attractions along the Jody River
changes to the Jody River
keys: What we have now are river taxis which tourists can board for a short ride along the Jody River
These warehouses of long ago have all been converted into shops, restaurants and banks.
It was built in the 1920s and used to be a school, but now it's been converted into a hotel which is popular with tourists.
qs.why: 'Mainly' means the whole talk: boats became river taxis, warehouses became shops, and a school became a hotel. It is all about changes. Collecting postcards is only the opening, and tourist attractions are only part of the talk.
qs.stem: Sarah's presentation is mainly about ______.
qs.key: What we have now are river taxis which tourists can board for a short ride along the Jody River

opts: They can individually defeat insects bigger than them.
They can make a new home by clumping together.
They can respond quickly to threats to their nest.
keys: By working together, they can very quickly bring down an insect many times their size.
During a flood, entire fire ant colonies can clump together and float until they find a new home.
The slightest disturbance to their nest will cause them to release chemical signals to warn one another so they can put up a defence within seconds.
qs.why: Option 1 is wrong: fire ants defeat bigger insects by working together, not individually. Option 2 is wrong: they clump together to float until they find a new home, not to build one. Option 3 is right: when their nest is disturbed they put up a defence within seconds.
qs.stem: Which of the following is true of fire ants?
qs.key: By working together, they can very quickly bring down an insect many times their size.

opts: They cause a burning sensation when they sting.
They damage homes and electrical equipment.
They are widely feared like fire.
keys: Fire ants attack by injecting a poisonous sting which causes a burning sensation, a painful reminder of how fire ants got their name.
qs.why: The answer is stated directly: the sting causes a burning sensation, a painful reminder of how fire ants got their name. 'Widely feared' is a result, not the reason for the name.
qs.stem: Why are fire ants named this way?
qs.key: Fire ants attack by injecting a poisonous sting which causes a burning sensation, a painful reminder of how fire ants got their name.

opts: dangerous
annoying
deadly
keys: These fiery stings have made the insect widely feared.
However, fire ants are more annoying than dangerous as people generally recover from these stings.
qs.why: 'Widely feared' comes before the word 'However'. After it, we hear that fire ants are more annoying than dangerous because people generally recover from the stings.
qs.stem: How do people generally view fire ants?
qs.key: These fiery stings have made the insect widely feared.

opts: He did not require the soldiers to report to him about their work.
He did not think that listening to reports was a waste of time.
He did not give away the rice free of charge.
keys: Unlike the queen, Prince Lawrence was lazy and impatient. He did away with listening to the soldiers' weekly reports.
qs.why: 'Unlike the queen' is followed by 'he did away with listening to the weekly reports'. Option 2 is the opposite: HE thought listening was a waste of time. Option 3 is not stated: it was Jasper who sold the rice.
qs.stem: In what way was Prince Lawrence different from the queen?
qs.key: Unlike the queen, Prince Lawrence was lazy and impatient. He did away with listening to the soldiers' weekly reports.

opts: He stole the rice to sell.
He kept the rice for himself.
He gave a little rice to the poor.
keys: At first, that was what Jasper did. However, stealing the rice soon became a habit he could not stop. Jasper even sold the rice at a high price to the needy.
qs.why: The question asks what eventually resulted. At first Jasper only kept a little rice for himself (option 2). Later stealing became a habit and he even sold the stolen rice at a high price to the needy.
qs.stem: What eventually resulted from Jasper's habit?
qs.key: At first, that was what Jasper did. However, stealing the rice soon became a habit he could not stop. Jasper even sold the rice at a high price to the needy.

opts: "Such a waste of my precious time!"
"The rice is supposed to be free!"
"You do have a loud voice for one so tiny!"
keys: Such a waste of my precious time!
Why are you fattening yourself at our expense? The rice is supposed to be free!
You do have a loud voice for one so tiny!
qs.why: The old woman is the angry one. She 'confronted' Jasper, which means she faced him and accused him. 'Fattening yourself at our expense' means: you are getting well-fed by taking what belongs to us, while we go without. She is blaming him for selling rice that should be free. The prince only 'moaned' (complained) and Jasper 'ridiculed' (made fun of) her.
qs.stem: Which statement was said in an angry way?
qs.key: Such a waste of my precious time!

opts: ashamed
distressed
humiliated
keys: In a quivering voice, Jasper asked, "Why are you giving me food when I denied you of it in the past?"
How could I not freely share it with you now?
qs.why: The old woman gives him food even though he denied her in the past, and says the Queen freely gave food, so she shares freely too. Jasper's voice quivers because he is ashamed of how he behaved. 'Humiliated' would mean someone made him feel small, and nobody did.
qs.stem: How did Jasper feel at the end of the story?
qs.key: In a quivering voice, Jasper asked, "Why are you giving me food when I denied you of it in the past?"

opts: asking if they have a grateful attitude
making a link between scientific proof and being grateful
sharing why it is important to study the advantages of being grateful
keys: Do you know that the benefits of being grateful are supported by scientific evidence?
qs.why: The first question links scientific evidence with the benefits of being grateful. He does not ask the audience if they are grateful, and he does not explain why studying it is important.
qs.stem: The programme captures the interest of the audience at the start by ______.
qs.key: Do you know that the benefits of being grateful are supported by scientific evidence?

opts: benefitted the needy
repaid those whom he was grateful to
led to the growth of charitable organisations
keys: For each thing or person he was grateful for, he would put a coin into a little box. When it became full, Ronnie would empty the coins and donate them to charity.
qs.why: Ronnie put coins in a box and donated them to charity, so the needy benefited. He did not repay people he was grateful to, and the talk does not say charities grew.
qs.stem: In the story about Ronnie, his daily practice ______.
qs.key: For each thing or person he was grateful for, he would put a coin into a little box. When it became full, Ronnie would empty the coins and donate them to charity.

opts: "A Grateful Person"
"Being Grateful Pays"
"Different Ways of Being Grateful"
keys: Some researchers found that being grateful can help us to be happier.
So then, how can we learn to be grateful?
Well, I hope my little story will encourage you to learn how to be a grateful person.
qs.why: The talk is mainly about the benefits of being grateful (happier, recover faster) and then how to learn it through Ronnie's story. 'Pays' here means 'brings benefits' or 'is worth it', not paying money. For example, 'Honesty pays' means being honest brings good results. So 'Being Grateful Pays' = being grateful has advantages. 'Different Ways' is wrong because only one way is shared, and 'A Grateful Person' sounds like a profile of one person.
qs.stem: Which is the most suitable title for this radio programme?
qs.key: Some researchers found that being grateful can help us to be happier.

texts.intro: You will hear a girl telling her friend about something that happened at home.
lines: Mei Ling, you look tired. What happened yesterday?

When I came home, the front gate was wide open. I thought my brother had forgotten to close it, so I wasn't worried. Then I saw muddy shoe prints in the hallway and my heart started to race. Finally, I found that my laptop was missing from the study table, so I called the police at once.
Oh no! What did the police find?
Nothing, actually. My brother had borrowed the laptop for school and left in a hurry. Looking back, it would have been wiser to phone him first instead of rushing to call the police. I felt so silly.

texts.intro: You will hear a radio host interviewing a swimming coach.
lines: Coach Ravi, your swimmers have won several medals this year. You must be pleased with their progress.

Of course. Some parents even ask me how soon their children can take part in competitions. However, not every child who joins my class dreams of becoming a champion. I once taught a boy who refused to put his face in the water. It took him several weeks before he could swim across the pool on his own. Watching him achieve that meant more to me than seeing another medal added to our collection.
What challenges do you face as a coach?

Getting up before sunrise took some getting used to, and dealing with demanding parents can be exhausting. Nevertheless, I've learnt to manage both. What I haven't found a solution to is the growing number of children whose schools are unable to provide swimming lessons. Some of these children may never get the opportunity to learn an important life skill.

texts.intro: You will hear a student talking to her teacher about the school garden.
lines: Mr Tan, I heard the flower beds are being dug up. Aren't the flowers popular? Everyone takes photos there.

They are, but they need watering twice a day, and the cooks in the canteen have been asking for fresh herbs and vegetables for years. We thought it would be a pity not to use the space for something the school can actually eat.
What about the water bill, then? Vegetables are thirsty too.
The vegetables we chose need much less water than the roses, so the bill will go down. I'll admit that wasn't why we decided, though. The cooks' request was.
Could we keep a few flowers?
A small corner, yes, if some students volunteer to look after them. Sign up with Miss Lim if you're interested.

texts.intro: You will hear two friends talking about a speech competition.
lines: I get so nervous speaking in front of the whole class.
Me too. Last term, I wrote my speech on small cards, but I still forgot my lines.
I tried practising in front of the mirror. It didn't help much. I just felt silly.
What worked for me was practising at the dinner table with my cousins. They kept interrupting with silly questions, and before I knew it, I had forgotten to be afraid.
Hmm, maybe I'll ask my sister to practise with me. I haven't decided yet.

qs.stem: When did Mei Ling first begin to feel worried?
opts: when she saw the muddy shoe prints
when she saw the open gate
when she found that her laptop was missing
keys: Then I saw muddy shoe prints in the hallway and my heart started to race.
qs.why: The question says FIRST. At the gate she was not worried. Her heart started to race at the shoe prints, which shows she was now worried. The missing laptop came later ('Finally').
qs.evidence: my heart started to race (= worried)
qs.reasoning: Infer the feeling from the physical reaction, and order the events.

wrong.2: She thought her brother had left it open, so she was not worried then.
wrong.3: This came after the shoe prints.

diag.2: May have missed 'wasn't worried': heard the first event but not her feeling. Follow-up: negation and feelings.
diag.3: May have ignored 'first' and chosen the most serious event. Follow-up: time limits (first, at first, initially).

qs.key: Then I saw muddy shoe prints in the hallway and my heart started to race.

qs.stem: What should Mei Ling have done?
opts: told the police that her brother might have the laptop
phoned her brother before calling the police
searched the rest of the house before calling the police
keys: Looking back, it would have been wiser to phone him first instead of rushing to call the police.
qs.why: The question asks what she SHOULD HAVE done, not what she did. 'Looking back, it would have been wiser' tells you the better choice: phone her brother first, before the police.
qs.limit: should have (what would have been wiser)
qs.evidence: it would have been wiser to phone him first
qs.reasoning: Match 'phone him first instead of ... the police' to the option.

wrong.1: Right idea (her brother) but wrong person: she should have asked him, not told the police.
wrong.3: Sounds sensible, but the script never says she should have searched the house.

diag.1: May have joined 'brother' and 'police' wrongly without working out who she should have talked to. Follow-up: who does what to whom.
diag.3: May have chosen a sensible-sounding action that is not in the script. Follow-up: answer only from what is said.

qs.key: Looking back, it would have been wiser to phone him first instead of rushing to call the police.

qs.stem: What can we learn from Mei Ling's experience?
opts: We should be more careful about keeping our belongings safe.
We should ask adults for help when we are worried.
We should check our assumptions before taking action.
keys: Looking back, it would have been wiser to phone him first instead of rushing to call the police.
I felt so silly.
qs.why: Her brother had only borrowed the laptop. She assumed the worst and called the police, then felt silly. She regrets not checking first, so the lesson is to check our assumptions before acting. Keeping belongings safe is only the background, and asking for help (she did call the police) is what she regrets doing too early.
qs.evidence: it would have been wiser to phone him first; I felt so silly
qs.reasoning: Combine the whole story into a lesson. The script never states it. She regrets acting on an assumption without checking.

wrong.1: The missing laptop is the event, not what she regrets.
wrong.2: She did ask for help (the police) and regrets doing it before checking.

diag.1: May have taken the surface event (the missing laptop) as the lesson. Follow-up: event vs lesson.
diag.2: May have chosen a general good habit without linking it to what she actually regrets. Follow-up: what does the speaker regret?

qs.key: Looking back, it would have been wiser to phone him first instead of rushing to call the police.

qs.stem: What gives Coach Ravi the greatest sense of satisfaction?
opts: discovering children with the potential to become champions
helping children overcome their fear of swimming
seeing his swimmers receive recognition for their achievements
keys: I once taught a boy who refused to put his face in the water.
Watching him achieve that meant more to me than seeing another medal added to our collection.
qs.why: The boy who refused to put his face in the water learnt to swim across the pool, and that 'meant more' to him than another medal. So the greatest satisfaction is helping a child overcome fear. Medals are recognition, which he values less. Parents asking about competitions is not about discovering champions.
qs.evidence: meant more to me than seeing another medal
qs.reasoning: Compare two things he mentions and decide which he values more. 'Fear' is never said; it is inferred from 'refused to put his face in the water'.

wrong.1: He says not every child dreams of becoming a champion; he does not say he looks for them.
wrong.3: Medals are recognition, and he says the boy's progress meant MORE.

diag.1: May have linked 'competitions' to 'champions' and missed 'not every child dreams of becoming a champion'.
diag.3: May have chosen the medals from the host's opening and missed 'meant more to me'. Follow-up: comparison words.

qs.key: I once taught a boy who refused to put his face in the water.

qs.stem: What is Coach Ravi most concerned about?
opts: the expectations parents have of children
the difficulty of managing his responsibilities
children's limited access to swimming lessons
keys: Nevertheless, I've learnt to manage both.
What I haven't found a solution to is the growing number of children whose schools are unable to provide swimming lessons.
qs.why: Early mornings and demanding parents are problems he has 'learnt to manage'. The problem he has not solved is that more children's schools cannot provide swimming lessons, so they have limited access.
qs.evidence: What I haven't found a solution to is ...
qs.reasoning: Separate problems he has handled from the one he has not solved. 'Limited access' paraphrases 'schools are unable to provide lessons'.

wrong.1: Parents ask about competitions and can be demanding, but that is not what he is most concerned about, and he has learnt to manage the demanding parents.
wrong.2: Getting up early and parents are things he has learnt to manage.

qs.skill: identifying the speaker's primary concern; distinguishing manageable problems from unresolved problems; contextual paraphrasing

diag.1: May have picked the parents option after hearing 'demanding parents' and missed that it is managed.
diag.2: May have picked the first problem listed and missed 'Nevertheless, I've learnt to manage both'.

qs.key: Nevertheless, I've learnt to manage both.

qs.stem: Why did the school decide to replace the flowers with vegetables?
opts: to lower the cost of watering
because few students visited the flower beds
to answer a request from the canteen staff
keys: We thought it would be a pity not to use the space for something the school can actually eat.
I'll admit that wasn't why we decided, though. The cooks' request was.
qs.why: Mr Tan says lower water cost was NOT why they decided. The reason was the cooks' request. 'Cooks in the canteen' means 'canteen staff'. The flowers were popular, so option 2 is wrong.
qs.evidence: I'll admit that wasn't why we decided, though. The cooks' request was.
qs.reasoning: A result (the bill goes down) is not the same as the reason. 'Cooks' = 'canteen staff'.

wrong.1: It is a result, and he says it was not the reason.
wrong.2: The flowers were popular; students took photos there.

diag.1: May have treated a result (lower bill) as the reason. Follow-up: cause vs result.
diag.2: May have assumed the flowers were unpopular simply because the school decided to remove them, despite explicit evidence to the contrary (unsupported assumption). Follow-up: separate personal assumptions from what the script says.

qs.key: We thought it would be a pity not to use the space for something the school can actually eat.

qs.stem: What has Mr Tan agreed to regarding the flowers?
opts: to remove all of the flowers
to keep a few if students help
to move them to Miss Lim's room
keys: A small corner, yes, if some students volunteer to look after them. Sign up with Miss Lim if you're interested.
qs.why: Mr Tan agrees to keep a small corner of flowers, but only on one condition: students must volunteer to look after them. So not every flower has to go, but keeping any is not guaranteed. Miss Lim is only the teacher to sign up with.
qs.evidence: A small corner, yes, if some students volunteer
qs.reasoning: Notice the condition (if) and the degree (a small corner).

wrong.1: Removal of all the flowers is not certain: some may remain if students volunteer to look after them.
wrong.3: Miss Lim is the person students should sign up with. There is no evidence that the flowers will be moved to her classroom.

diag.1: May have remembered 'dug up' and ignored 'yes, if'. Follow-up: conditions.
diag.3: May have attached a name heard nearby (Miss Lim) to the wrong thing. Follow-up: who or what a name belongs to; not mentioned vs stated as false.

qs.key: A small corner, yes, if some students volunteer to look after them. Sign up with Miss Lim if you're interested.

qs.stem: What helped Ben overcome his nervousness?
opts: Having written reminders of his speech.
Rehearsing in front of a mirror.
Interacting with a familiar audience.
keys: What worked for me was practising at the dinner table with my cousins. They kept interrupting with silly questions, and before I knew it, I had forgotten to be afraid.
qs.why: Ben's cards (written reminders) did not stop him forgetting his lines, and the mirror was Aisha's attempt. What worked was practising with his cousins, who kept interrupting with silly questions, so he forgot to be afraid. 'Familiar audience' means people he knows well, such as cousins.
qs.evidence: What worked for me was practising at the dinner table with my cousins
qs.reasoning: 'Cousins' = 'familiar audience'. Separate what he tried that failed (cards) and what Aisha tried (mirror) from what worked.

wrong.1: He wrote his speech on cards, but he still forgot his lines.
wrong.2: The mirror was Aisha's attempt, and she said it did not help her.

qs.skill: what worked vs what was tried; paraphrase

diag.1: May have chosen a method that was mentioned but did not work. Follow-up: what was tried vs what worked.
diag.2: May have given Aisha's attempt to Ben (speaker attribution). Follow-up: who said what.

qs.key: What worked for me was practising at the dinner table with my cousins. They kept interrupting with silly questions, and before I knew it, I had forgotten to be afraid.

qs.stem: What is Aisha considering doing next?
opts: asking her sister to practise with her
writing her speech on small cards
practising in front of the mirror again
keys: Hmm, maybe I'll ask my sister to practise with me. I haven't decided yet.
qs.why: Aisha says 'maybe' and 'I haven't decided yet', so asking her sister is only something she is considering. The mirror is what she already tried, and the cards were Ben's idea.
qs.evidence: maybe I'll ask my sister ... I haven't decided yet
qs.reasoning: Match the certainty of the question ('considering') with 'maybe'.

wrong.3: She already tried the mirror and said it did not help.

qs.skill: degree of certainty; past vs future

diag.2: May have given Ben's cards to Aisha (speaker attribution).
diag.3: May have taken a past attempt as the next plan (chronology). Follow-up: past vs future.

qs.key: Hmm, maybe I'll ask my sister to practise with me. I haven't decided yet.

keyword.label: Key Word in the Question
keyword.tip: Every option may be mentioned in the text, so hearing a word is not enough. Underline the limiting word in the question first (first / last / right after / start again / should have / finally / most / at the start). Then listen for the verb or the order that matches it.

2025-2.why: The rule says you may stick out one leg or both hands. 'Stick out' means to put a body part outside the hoop. But if BOTH feet are out of the hoop, you are disqualified. Picture 1: the boy on the left has both feet outside the hoop, so he is breaking the rule. Picture 2: only one foot is out, which is allowed. Picture 3: both feet are inside and only his hands are outside, which is allowed.
